Future is coming, I can understand safety concerns but there shouldn't be people saying we should slow down an industry until there is real data on whether their fears are justified.

The article is basically just this quote:

And so they are turning the automobile into an ever more complicated computer on wheels. Which means that the driver is losing control to the software, and the more the driver loses control to the software, the less the driver is going to be able to control the car down the road.

I'm trying to think of some downsides here but I really can't-- at least once all the kinks are worked out.

As a developer I'll tell you the downsides. It was programmed by humans, under deadlines, and stressed. Or possibly it was programmed by bad developers cause they couldn't pay the same rate Facebook or Google was paying for good devs. Or a ton of reasons but it all comes back to the fact that the people that made it are still just humans that are prone to errors.

Eventually it will be good enough..ish and the developers will start having to work on features that marketing feels are more important to add in to sell more units over making sure stuff is perfect.

Marketing director: So we have been getting a lot of customer complaints about the cars staying in the same lane for a long time.

Engineer: The cars network with each other to calculate an optimal traffic pattern, which results in very few lane changes.

Marketing director: Well some of our customers feel like they could get to their destination faster if the faster cars could pass the slower cars. Right now it is simply unsatisfactory.

Engineer: I don't understand what you want. The cars calculate the best possible route and the path is within 5% of the optimal network solution. Do you want me to add a setting so the passengers can change lanes more often?

Marketing director: You can do that? Make them change lanes more often? That would be great! How long will that take? If you could build that into the systems before next week we could talk about it at the big Expo.
You want to cause rage? Devise a car that cannot accelerate to any speed faster than what is posted on the sign.

That would cause rage if the posted speed was what we typically see today. Then it would be a matter of expectations, cars are able to go faster than 55, or 75, so sometimes drivers want to go faster, too. If you posted "Max Speed 200 MPH" and physically limited cars from going faster, only the most pedantic folks would complain, and most drivers would still go only, perhaps, 90 mph.

Think about it this way, have you ever bought a computer that suddenly crashed seemingly out of the blue. Yes? Well, in the future computers will still do this; only this time when they crash, your car will crash along with it.

Well, 90% of crashes are due to driver error. Multiple studies show self driving cars would greatly reduce accidents.

But then you will get the occasion where aomething goes wrong. Ever been on an over pass and your gps advises you to turn? What if the computer is processing wrong in that specific rate set of circumstances and you drive off the overpass and ontop of another car, causing multiple fatalities? That's what Ralph is worried about- new issues which remain to be seen.

I personally think the rollout is going too slow, we saw aelf parallel parking years ago. But I see Ralph's point that we have not had a large enough testing base to go out today selling driverless cars to grandma.

But the point is if you become an alert skilled driver you can greatly increase your chances of surviving on the road. With a self driving car you are playing roulette; the person in the car would have no say. You should also be skeptical of "multiple studies" showing that self driving cars would greatly reduce accidents. For one thing such cars are not available in large enough numbers to generate any sort of statistics that are comparable to modern cars. They also don't take into account potential new vulnerabilities such as hacking that can create potentially millions of instantaneous deaths in the new system that are impossible in the current one. And of course, many of these studies are being funded by the car manufacturers themselves to promote their agenda (independent agencies don't have access to the data on the cars yet because most of them are still prototypes).

I don't want a self-driving car. If that means I have to hire some Cubans to keep a 53 Buick in repair so I can drive it, so be it. There would be nothing more completely awful than a car that automatically obeys whatever instruction given to it by the government.
